The Times — Thursday 24 September 2026, 3.52pm BST. By Oliver Wright, Policy Editor.
[BACKGROUND / CONTEXT ONLY — published Thursday, well before the 18:00 Friday cut-off. Use for context on Chagos, not as a new lead. No Mauritius response or FCDO statement found in the last 14 hours.]

HEADLINE: Chagos deal is dead after Trump opposition, ministers believe
Standfirst: Whitehall source admitted that it would be hard for Andy Burnham to negotiate a new agreement that pleased both Mauritius and the US

FACTS:
- Plans to hand the Chagos Islands over to Mauritius are "dead" and will have to be renegotiated after President Trump reiterated his opposition, ministers believe.
- Senior government sources said ministers were under "no illusion" that the existing deal, signed by Keir Starmer last year, could be resurrected. Officials are preparing to restart negotiations with Mauritius to reach a new deal acceptable to the White House.
- One source said it might be possible to make "cosmetic" changes to the agreement, citing the deal Trump signed with Denmark reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over Greenland.
- The deal terms: Britain would pay £165 million a year for three years, then £120 million for 96 years, to lease back the joint US/UK airbase on Diego Garcia.
- The deal was announced by Starmer in October 2024 but delayed after Trump returned to the White House the following year.
- The US position changed after Starmer initially denied the US access to the base to attack Iranian positions over concerns the war was not legal.
- A UN vote in 2019, supported by Russia, China and Venezuela, awarded the islands to Mauritius, whose claim was then approved by a 13-1 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice.
- Trump made clear both in public and in private during his meeting with Burnham on Tuesday that his position had not changed.
- One Whitehall source said the agreement with Mauritius was made under a previous government and Burnham did not feel bound by it.

QUOTE (unnamed senior government source): "We are going to have to go back to the drawing board. The challenge is keeping the Mauritians onboard."
QUOTE (Whitehall source): "We will certainly try - but what we cannot do is keep the current deal on hold. That is not sustainable any longer."

QUOTE (Wes Streeting, Defence Secretary, speaking on Wednesday to Times Radio): the deal "can't go ahead without American support". On the ICJ ruling: while it was "advisory now, there is a potential further course of legal action avenue open to the government of Mauritius".
QUOTE (Wes Streeting): "I'm not pretending that's an easy position and that resolving this is not going to be difficult. It is difficult and necessarily painstaking work, but it is necessary."
QUOTE (Wes Streeting): "The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it [will] go away, I would caution, is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world."
